0.long_answer: The most common type of congenital dyserythropoietic anemia is congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II (CDA II). This subtype is characterized by a distinct bone marrow morphology with numerous binucleated or multinucleated erythroblasts and is caused by mutations in the SEC23B gene, following an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. CDA II is often referred to as HEMPAS (hereditary erythroblastic multinuclearity with a positive acidified serum lysis test). More than 200 cases have been described, making it the most frequently encountered form among the congenital dyserythropoietic anemias.

1.long_answer: Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II (CDA II) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the SEC23B gene. This gene mutation disrupts the normal function of the SEC23B protein, which plays a crucial role in the transport of proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus. The disruption of this pathway impairs the maturation and proper development of red blood cells, leading to the ineffective erythropoiesis and the characteristic bone marrow abnormalities observed in CDA II.
